title: Token Concerto: latency harmonizer and attention pathfinder
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Goal: Reduce 95th/99th token latency for multi-tenant continuous-batching workloads by coordinating dynamic kernel selection, attention execution paths, and prefill/decode admission policies.

Problem statement: We observe intermittent tail spikes for mixed-length request streams under continuous batching. Root causes appear to be mismatches between batch-shape assumptions and the kernel chosen at admission time, and attention fallback paths for long prefixes that trigger slower kernels mid-decode. Current admission uses coarse heuristics that over-commit slots or pick a generic kernel profile, causing late kernel swaps and KV cache misses.

Approach: Implement a three-part system (Token Concerto):
1) Fast kernel probing at admission: perform a lightweight micro-benchmark (kernel probe) using the request's length/metadata to select a kernel variant before committing slots. Probing must be sub-millisecond and run on the scheduler thread; fall back to safe kernel if probe fails.
2) Attention pathfinder: add a predecode analysis that predicts whether the attention execution will remain in the short/medium/long path based on prefix tokens + sampling of recent tokens in the tenant's workload. If the pathfinder predicts a long attention trace, we preselect fused attention kernels and reserve KV-friendly memory layouts to avoid mid-decode swaps.
3) Graceful admission + batch shaping: extend admission controller to allow soft reservations with a prefill tier and a decode tier. Prefill slots can be temporarily scaled down (deferred) when probe signals kernel budget pressure. Introduce a small token-level re-ordering window (3–5ms) to coalesce similar shape requests without violating latency SLOs.

Trade-offs and constraints:
- Probing adds CPU overhead on the scheduler; must be bounded (<0.8ms/request) and sampled for low-risk tenants.
- Conservative kernel selection increases steady-state latency for some short streams; mitigated by targeted routing and dynamic rollback.
- Re-ordering window can improve throughput but may increase P95 slightly for corner cases; we will gate by tenant SLO and offer opt-out.

Implementation plan:
- Phase A: Implement kernel probe shim + microbench harness (scheduler-side), feature-flag gated. (ENG side: scheduler, kernel-chooser).
- Phase B: Build attention-path predictor model (lightweight rule-based first, then telemetry-trained classifier). Expose prediction to admission API.
- Phase C: Admission extension: implement soft reservations, token-level re-ordering window, connector to cache pre-allocations.
- Phase D: Canary rollout with telemetry and automatic rollback thresholds.

Metrics to collect during rollout: P50/P95/P99 token latency, decode-stage latency, kernel-swap rate, KV-cache hit ratio, CPU overhead per admission, throughput (tokens/s).

Success criteria: measurable tail reduction (see acceptance_criteria), stable CPU and memory overheads, no increase in customer errors or incorrect outputs due to re-ordering.
acceptance_criteria: P95 token latency reduced by >= 12% on mixed-length internal benchmark compared to baseline (runtime-1.20) at target load
P99 token latency reduced by >= 8% on same benchmark
Kernel swap rate during decodes reduced by >= 60%
KV-cache hit ratio improved by >= 10% for tenants enabled in canary
Scheduler CPU overhead for probing below 0.8ms per request on 95% of samples
Canary rollout shows no increase in "errors" or model regressions attributable to re-ordering window (defined by quality regression alerts)
